blocks.x: Okay, I believe it's going all right now. This is an interview being recorded at 600 Charter Street. And what's today's date? Lemon, you remember October the...
It's October the 3rd.
Yeah, it's October the 3rd, 1959. That's right. And my name is Dick Allen. What's yours, Lemon?
My name is Lemon Nash.
Okay, Bill, do you want to talk a little? You're going to be quiet. I'll keep quiet. I'm over here. What's your name? Bill Russell, what is your full name? Lemon Nash.
Do you have any middle name? No, just Lemon Nash.
And how was your name spelled?
L-E-M-O-N-N-S-H.
That's the original spelling?
That's right. L-E-M-O-N-N-S-H.
I see. And where were you born?
I was born in Lakeland, but I was brought here when I was a baby.
That's Lakeland, Louisiana? That's right. And how old were you, you say?
I was born in 1898, April 22nd. This next birth I'll be 62. I mean next April. The 22nd.
And how old were you when you were brought to the city?
I was around about two months old.
Oh, quite young then.
Yeah.
And how long have you lived here? All the time since?

Well, I've been here. I stayed here around about 20 years and I left here and went to Chicago, Detroit. I used to be on the medicine shows. Used to work in theaters and so on. Sideshows and the circus. John Robinson Circus. I was with Downey Brothers, Sells and Floteau. I was with the big chief Indian selling medicine out through the country.
Oh, well you've been done quite a bit of traveling. Oh yes, I did a lot of that. What's the earliest music or singing that you remember?

Well, the first blues I ever heard was St. Louis Blues. To remember, the first blues I've heard was St. Louis Blues. Then I've heard a lot of other old songs. Songs like, Who Stole a Lock Off the Hen House Door. I heard a song about Big Rock Candy Mountain. And I heard the song about K.C. John, Steamboat Bill. And another old song I used to sing around New Orleans years ago when I was a kid. He'd sing that song about Winter Night and the Junkman Rag. And all those old songs way back here. And songs, old quartet song. Old quartet used to sing songs about shots and shells are ringing on the battlefield. And another song they used to sing about when sailing over the mountain hill. Many storm and wind shall blow when Jack come home again. All those old numbers.
How old were you when you heard St. Louis Blues, Lemma?

Well, I must have been around about eight years old when I heard the St. Louis Blues. I was about eight. I had an uncle who played a mandolin. One played a guitar. And another uncle played a bass. Bass violin. And one of my uncles used to sing.
I see. What were their names?

Well, one named Fred Nan Callender. And what did he play? He played a mandolin. And the others? One named Fred Callender. He played the guitar. And you had one more? Yeah, I had another one. One they called Joseph Callender. He played a bass. And my uncle Willie Callender used to sing. Yeah, that's the four of them. And were they here in the city? Yeah, they was all around here. But they was partly raised around Plaquemine, Louisiana, out here. The road there in this piece. But they used to be here.
And did they perform just as a group themselves or would they play with other bands?
Well, no. They just had a group of themselves, you know, just brothers.
What about your father? Did he play?
Well, my father used to play accordion years ago. So they said, but I was too young to know anything about it. Because I was a baby when he died, you know. My daddy died.
What kind of songs would your uncles play? All those that you named or brothers?

Well, yeah. Those numbers I named, they used to play those numbers. St. Louis Blues. They played K.C. John. Steamboat Bill. That Oughta Get It. And they played the Junk Man Rag. And they played Shots and Shells Are Rain On The Battlefield. And they used to play I Had A Dream. I Had A Dream. And they played the... Over there. Send a word to the boys over there. They're always in World War I.
How did that Junk Man Rag go? Do you remember any words to it?

No, I can't get the words, but I know it's the air. The music of it is strange. Can you remember it this low? Yeah, mm-hmm. It goes... D-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d Can you play that on the U? Well I used to but it's been quite a while since I tried to play that. Well I can learn it. I can learn it in a couple of hours or so and I can do practice it. Junkman Rag, that's an old, old number.
Now you mentioned that all together. What is that like?

I think Steve Luce made a recorded record of that, That Oughta Get It. That's where they go. Did it have words on there? Yeah it had words too. I just can't remember. Steve Luce recorded a record of that. Used to play out here on Charler Street.
Where did he play?
He played piano.
Yeah but where? What plays?
Around there on Charler Street. Used to play, I'll tell you where he played, right on Toulouse and Charler. You know where they got the piano in the corner place? Across from the restaurant?
You mean Victor's Ball right there?
That's right. That's what Steve Luce used to play. Is that right? That's right. He used to play that. That's been a long time.
Well what other music did you hear before you started playing yourself?
Well, what kind of music did I hear?
Yeah, before you started playing yourself.

Well, I heard there used to be an old band around here called the New Orleans Dixie Stompers or something. I can't just remember the name but they had a saxophone, a bass, violin, and a guitar. That's been a long, long time. I can't even remember the guy's name but it's been a long time. That was way back in, that was right around back from 19, 19, 8. Around in 19, 8.
Do you remember any of the other guys? Huh? Who were some of the other early musicians you remember?

Well, after that then Sam Morgan. I mean Celestine was about the only best band that I could really remember around here, Papa Celestine. And then after Papa Celestine then it was Sam Morgan. After Sam Morgan then Chris Kelly had a band. After Chris Kelly then it was Buddy P.T. He had a band, played a trumpet. After Buddy P.T. then Kid Ran A. He up with a band. But Papa Celestine and Lou Armstrong, about the oldest two bands that I know around here. That's right, Papa Celestine and Lou Armstrong.
Well did you hear many guys walking around serenading? Oh yeah, yeah.

A lot of guys. I used to serenade myself. After I used to play mandolin, you know. Yeah. Yeah. Well, there's a fella around here that call him Battle House. He's around here. He's one of the lead serenaders. Yeah. I met him the day before yesterday. Now uptown. He sure was glad to see me. He picked the guitar, you know. Picked all them old breakdowns and things. You know, he used to play for those fish fries. Wherever you see a lantern hanging outside the house with the red paper over it, it had fish fry there. Selling fried fish. So that's how Battle House earned his living. You know, he made them fish fries playing guitar. Who is that guy? He's uptown. Nah, I wouldn't know where he lived, but he's one of the house party kings, you know, on the fish fry. They call him Battle House. Everybody in town knows him. Yeah. Yeah, they call him Battle House. The reason why they give him that name is he used to drink so much corn liquor, moonshine liquor, you know. Homebrew. And of course, way back in them days, they had that old sweet lucid wine and all that stuff, you know. He used to drink and fall on the floor anywhere and go to sleep. That's not Battle House. No, Battle House. I know Battle House. I'm the first one taught Battle House a chord on the guitar. No, Battle House, he fix televisions and he plays over here on Bourbon Street there. Yeah. Yeah, by a quarter of two sisters. I know. Now I'm talking about this Battle House. That's what they call them, Battle House.
What is, what is Battle House special in? What kind of numbers?

Well, Battle House, well he had a piece he used to play about, I wished I had a nickel, I wished I had a dime. If I had fifteen cents I'd buy some wine. That was his favorite number. That's right. And he used to drink it, huh? Yeah. Uh huh.
Yeah, he used to drink it, see. If I had a nickel, I wish I had a dime. If I had fifteen cents I'd buy some wine.

Well, if you could find his address for me, I'd sure he would appreciate it. Well, I'll try. I believe I can get it. You can see him, I'm sure. Yeah, I'm sure I'll find him. I'd appreciate it very much. He's uptown there and all I got to do is ask somebody where he lived and they're going
to show me and they're going to tell me where he lived. Yeah, he's one of the old fish fry or one of the old serenaders around there.

I asked him the other day, did he still play? Keeps it for a souvenir, I guess. Well, how, what kind of style of guitar did he play? Did he use a piano? I guess I'd buy some wine. I'd buy some wine. Well, if you could find his address for me, I'd sure he'd appreciate it. Well, I'll try. I believe I can get it. Yeah, he's one of the old fish fry or one of the old serenaders around there. I asked him the other day, did he still play? He said, no, so he put it down and said, but he keeps his guitar around there, you know. Keeps it for a souvenir, I guess.
Well, what kind of style of guitar did he play? Did he use a pick or a finger?
No, he used his finger. Finger man. Would be interested now. Yeah, that's what he used, his fingers. Never could use a pick, nothing but his fingers. He picked everything.
Well, now you yourself, when did you start serenading?
Well, I started serenading back around in 19, let me see, 1922.
Had you had any lessons?

Well, I used to fool around a musician, they taught me a few things. Fester Monette crossed the river. And I used to be with one of the best guitar players in town, they called him Frank Wagner. He hung himself. He was working on the P.W.A., things got rough around there and he couldn't support his mother like he wanted, so he just tied a rope around his neck. And he got, stood on a box, tied a rope around his neck and kicked the box from under him. And he fell on his neck and hung himself right uptown there. He was one of the swell guitar players, he used to pick all them nice marches and all that. That's right, I used to play with him. There you go. Well, Frank Wagner used to live on sixth, let me see, he lived on sixth street between Howard, let me see, sixth street between Howard and Liberty. That's where he used to live. In fact, I believe that's why he hung himself. I see. Did he play with bands? Well, the most time he played two, three pieces, mandolin, ukulele and guitar. Sometime a bass guitar and ukulele. I used to play with him. We used to go all around, you know, and all around the French market and all down on Decatur Street and uptown, Auschannel, all around. We used to go around and play, you know. That's way back in, oh, I'd say around 21 and 22, up in there.
What was your first instrument?

My first instrument was the guitar was my first instrument. So I quit playing the guitar and started fooling the mandolin. So I stayed on the ukulele. I never did quit the ukulele. I stayed there with the ukulele.
I see. And how old were you when you took up guitar?

When I took up guitars around about 13 years old. Around up in the 13. How long did you play it? Well, I played it around about, and I got about 16, 17. I'll say 17. Then I started playing the ukulele. Ukulele is so famous around here, out at the beach and different places. So I started, I was working at Morris Music Shop there, you know. I used to sell ukuleles there for them, you know, and doing the Christmas holidays and so on. And so I just stayed on the ukulele. Stayed on the ukulele.
And, okay, let's see now. How long were you on the mandolin, did you say?

I was on, well, I was on the mandolin just a short a while. I'll say about three, four months. But then I left the mandolin, went to the, I left the guitar, went to the mandolin, but I left the mandolin. I saw everybody playing the ukulele, so it seemed like they all liked the ukulele, so I got with the ukulele.
I see. Did you ever play banjo?
Well, yeah, I played the banjo a little too. I played a little banjo too. In fact, the first ukulele I bought was a banjo ukulele.
I see. When was it you played the banjo itself, the tenor banjo? The tenor banjo?
The tenor banjo? Oh, around in, around in 25, 1925. I got married in 26. No, it wasn't, in 25 I got married, that's right, 25.
Did you play the guitar professionally?
Well, I made a living at it when I was playing.
Alone or with a band?
Well, when I was playing, we had a little four piece band, five piece sometimes. I used to play with Peter Williams.
Who is he?
That's one of the old Dixieland musicians back on, he lived back on Gravy Street between White and Gauza. No, White and Dupree. White and Dupree. He lived on Gravy Street between White and Dupree.
That's back around James Allen.

That passed just two blocks, one block across James Allen. That's where Rabbit used to hang out. That's right. I know Rabbit. That's right. I played with Rabbit a couple of times, but Rabbit played so bad I had to let him go.
He played bad?

Yeah, he was mad, mad. Rabbit just hit the guitar and hollered. I mean his coat tail, he had a frock tail coat he used to wear, and that coat tail would be just sailing. He was what you call a clown man. He used to go out all out that, had mama loose, and things get tough out that, he didn't make no money. He'd call up the fire wagon, you know, and he knew all the guys was on the fire wagon. And he'd give them a false alarm, they'd all get out there and there wouldn't be no fire. And Rabbit would say, hey, how about riding back in town with y'all? That's how Rabbit is getting back. That's right. That's just the way he's getting back. I mean they got some old timers here to tell you all about it. But that's what them tell you. That's how rabbits get back in town.
Well he made that tune, James Alley, did you ever hear the record of it?
No, I never heard of it.
Someday I'll play it for you. Yeah? Well he had some special numbers too, didn't he?
Well he used to sing, he had a record number, he used to sing about the downfall of the line.
And who was the line?

Yeah, the downfall of the line, the time they had all that shooting down there when, what you call him, got killed. What did they call him? That Italian got killed that time. The chief, when the chief got killed. That's Chief David Hennessey. That's right, Chief Hennessey. That's right, when Rabbit made a song about that. That was the downfall, yeah, who killed the chief, his downfall of the line. Yeah, he had all kinds of songs on it. We talked about that before.
We want to find August sometime, his nephew in Chicago. No, August dead.

August is dead? I just got a message, he died. Do you know that was the first fella I played with? You brought my remembers. The rabbit's little nephew, August, played a mandolin. He and I was the first two young fellas around, they used to go around and certainly, just two of us. I played guitar and he played mandolin. August died, a fella, I met his uncle. His uncle told me that he died, it must be true, so he died in Chicago.
You reckon his uncle would remember any of those songs?
Well, maybe so. Maybe so. I see his uncle quite often. His uncle's always passing the Jackson and Drive. I see him a lot.
You ought to get that down pat, that down follow the line, that would be worth having.
Sure do.
That would be wonderful. You know, that's the history of New Orleans right now.
Oh yeah, I know it.
So August was the first one. You never did know August's last name, huh?
No, I forget it. Been so long, he left here and went to Chicago and he stayed away so long I really forgot his last name. But I can get it to his uncle, you know.
Sure, we'd like to know that. I know Richard Brown was Rabbit's name.
Uh huh, that's right. That was his name, Richard Brown. Sure was. I remember Rabbit's name very well. Because Rabbit used to live in the battlefield, you know.
What's a battlefield?
The battlefield, that's on Lafayette. That's on Lafayette between Clara and Willow. That's right at the heart of the battlefield.
From Lafayette between Clara and Willow.

Yeah, it's a big brick road. A brick road, low, low, low box steps down there. But it's an old brick building. All that thing been there for years. And Illinois Central had a White House back there. I didn't know I ain't been back there in so long. I guess they been tanned down so much. I guess they probably didn't tore that place down.
Was it a nice, quiet neighborhood?

Oh man, them guys was tough out there. All them guys had 16 shooter Winchester. That's why they called it the battlefield. Guys so tough out there. Whenever they had a humbug in the battlefield, you couldn't get the peace. You couldn't get that, you called the laws up. They wasn't gone out there in the battlefield. Them guys was bad out there. And they had a gang of them Peen brothers out there. Thomas Peen, he got killed. Thomas Peen, Harry Peen, Willie Peen. All them guys was hogs out there. Bad, you know. And the other fella, they called him String Bean. Tall, slim fella. Guy never about to touch that ceiling when he stand up. That's right. They used to call him String Bean. Some guys called him Big Long Boy. Yeah, called him Long Boy. He died too.
Did anybody ever get hurt out there?

Oh, several fellas got cut. They had one fella trying to pistol out, shot in the fire after the bullet glanced back and killed him. Jim. That's right. Did him right in his stomach. Boy by the name of, what that boy name again? I know his name. They said we could pass for twin brothers. That's how much we favored. Brother Grant. Brother Grant. That was his name. Shot in the fire half, I believe, and they had a steel sheet. Sheet iron in the fire half to protect the bricks. You know where they had burned all out and shot down his bullet, glanced right back, hot, and hit him. He died before he got to the hospital.
Let's see, after you worked with August, who did you work with?

Well, after I worked with August, I worked with Cyun, a violin player. He's an old timer too. He lived in Baton Rouge, you know. We used to play all out of the canal in front, that Eddie Woodruff place. You know where he is? Walter Coren, the one that had the position in the custom house. We used to play for all their parties. They used to throw on big parties. There's La Youn, the violin player. He lived in Baton Rouge.
What part of Baton Rouge does he live in?

I can go right to his house, but I couldn't tell you. Some of the streets I know in Baton Rouge, like Alabama Street, Louisa Street, East Boulevard, Highland Road, and Floyd Street. I know where that's at. Then they got another street in Baton Rouge I know too. They had Posey Street in Baton Rouge. Then they had, at that time they had another street in Baton Rouge called, what street is that? Cozy, Posey Street. Then they had, I can't think of the name of that street.
Does he live around Scotlandville or close in than that?

No, he don't live very far from Louisa Street. It's a fella got a place out there in Baton Rouge they call the APEC. It's a ballroom. Anybody in that APEC that you ever catch in the APEC going to show you where Sa Youn lives. Sa Youn don't live far from that. Well he's one of the old violin players of New Orleans. We all played together. He played violin. We had a violin, ukulele, and I had another boy who played a mandolin with me, Johnny Bynum. He died in Baton Rouge. He and I traveled all over together playing. I was playing guitar then. We had a guitar and mandolin. We had a fella play bass we met in Nashville, Tennessee. But he finally came to the bad news and he died. He died here about, Johnny been dead now two years ago. I met a fella on canal in Rampart. Told me, say, you know Johnny play, a fella played beautiful mandolin. You and him used to play this? He said, yeah. He said, they just buried him last week. I mean, about two years ago. Let me see now.
Let me turn it off a second. You tell him about you played with Sa Youn and Bynum was with you? Mm-hmm. And all that, okay? Yeah. And then what happened?

Well, me and Sa Youn, Frank Wagner, we was the lady that had a Jose. Jose. Jose played bass with us. That's right. He's in California now, Los Angeles. He's an old timer. Oh, he must be about, Jose about 70. Jose 50, 60, 70. Jose must be about 88 years old now, but he's still playing the bass.
Jose's still playing the bass out there?
That's right, in California. That's right. He left here and went to Los Angeles.
What's his full name?
All I know is Jose. I can't think of that other name.

Well, I'd love to find an 88 year old bass player. Yeah. What part of California? Los Angeles. Los Angeles, yeah. That's right. Well, we'll find him, somehow. Johnny St. Seah ought to know where he is. I bet you they know each other.
Johnny's in Los Angeles too, yeah. I bet Johnny, I know Johnny doesn't found him since he's been out there. I'm sure he is. That would be great.
We can find him too, man. You know more people all over. Yeah. I got a fella right now, play bass with me.

He's 80 some years old. He's 88. I mean, play much rhythm as you want to hear. Papa John. We've been practicing last week. Remember, I got a nice little set up now, full pieces. John Joseph. Yeah, that's right. They call him Papa John.
Joseph.

You know him, huh? Well, sure. Well, he's 88, I heard. I heard he's 88. He's 88. Well, he changes his age from day to day. But he's gotta be up in his 80s or 90s. Yeah, he's a hundred and a hundred. Well, let's see.

You got August with you first. You were with him. How long were you with August? Well, August and I, we played around together. I'd say around about six years, around here. Then finally August left, went Chicago.
August went to Chicago. He was a big fan of Chicago.

He was a big fan of Chicago. He was a big fan of Chicago. He was a big fan of Chicago. He was a big fan of Chicago. He left here. How long were you with August? August and I, we played around together.
I'll say around about six years, around here. Then finally August left, went to Chicago. August went to Chicago. That was around in 20- . 22- . 23- . . . . 22 or 23 he left here.
And how long were you with Cyune?
Oh, I played around here at Cyune for long, the whole time he was here, until he moved to Baton Rouge. Yeah, I played with him a long time around here.
And that's after August left with Chicago?
That's right, after August left with Chicago.
I see. And after Cyune, then who?
After Cyune, and I got with Peter William.
And who was in that band?

Well, they was practically all young fellas. Me and Peter was about the two oldest in the band. And I can't remember those guys. Yeah, we had a little fella, he died in California, played a beautiful trumpet. Called him George, Kid George. Yeah, he died in California, played trumpet with us. I was playing guitar banjo at that time, six-string banjo, what I was playing.
And what did Peter Williams play?
He played drums.
Good clarinet player?

Yeah, well, no, he don't play no clarinet. He played, we had a clarinet play all right, but Peter played drums, George played trumpet, I played guitar banjo. And this other, had one guy that played saxophone, and one played clarinet.
Remember their names?

Yeah, I can't remember those two guys' names. Only three of the guys I remember. It was Peter, Kid George, and, yeah. And where we had, you see, we had Fan playing piano. Fan, I can't think of that boy's name. He plays a banjo. You know Fan? Well, Fan, Fan have played with us.
Fan bourgeois.
Yeah, that's right, Fan bourgeois, man. You have a bass player? Fan bourgeois. No, we had no bass.
Trombone?
No, we had no trombone.
And how long you said that?
We played at the Shell, at the Shell building over there.
Where is that?
That's right there. That's on Common. Common? Common is what? Dry and Common. Dry and Common. Right on the corner, Dry and Common. But on the downtown side.
I keep wanting to ask you about...
You know, to add on to the Roosevelt Hotel, you know?
Yeah.
Well, that add on, that's why we played the Shell people. You know what, the Shell motor people. Well, there they give power. We played there. Let me see. We played three dances there.
To get back to August and Cyun, what kind of jobs did you play with them?
Well, we played party jobs, you know, entertaining. We played a few dances, too.
And how would that work, though, when you mentioned serenading? How does that work?

Well, sometimes we would tip on the porch and start playing. The door would fly open. They'd say, come on in, boys. Come on in. I'm glad you're all here. That's serenading, you know? And we played parties, you know? They'd come and get us. Tell us, well, we'd like to have the four of you tonight. Play.
Would you ever go in a saloon and play for dips?

Well, yeah. We'd go anywhere. We ain't had no special place. Anywhere we could get a dollar, we'd go there and play. I see. Anywhere. Ballroom. Patio. We had guys used to just ride us around. We'd play while they ride and all that kind of stuff.
What would you be riding in?
Well, we'd be riding a big car. We'd be sitting in the back. They'd be sitting in the front. We'd be just playing the music for them. All right. They'd listen.
I never heard of that.

That's right. I've done that. All right. That Columbus, Tennessee. The guy must have ride me and Johnny Bynum about, oh, must have rid us about 80 or 90 miles just to listen to us play. I was playing the ukulele. Johnny was playing the mandolin that time. And he plays wonderful mandolin. And the guys, you know, they'd just give us $10 a piece and say, don't forget, boys, you're going to get some more. We just want you to play for us. So we're going over here and we want our girlfriend to hear y'all. Take us at that house. We'd play some there for a girl. We'd go to the other house. Then they'd bring us back. We'd play all along the highway. Play for them. All that.
I see. Well, with Cyune, would you walk around?

Yeah. Yeah. Cyune's cast violin. Had on his tux. I had my guitar. At least my ukulele. Frank Wagner had his guitar. Three-piece combination. Violin, guitar, and ukulele. We get a dance, then we go get a bass player. With a high bass player.
Well, now, let's see. After Peter Williams came, huh?

After Peter Williams? After I came, I mean, I came to Peter Williams after these guys. These guys way back in, way back in, oh, this way back around 19, around 19, let me see, around 1910 and nine, 19, nine, up in nine, them years.
Yeah, but who did you play with after you played with Peter Williams?
After I played with him?
Mm-hmm.
Oh, I played with Peter Williams and Kid George, trumpet player. Peter played drums. Had one guy play the saxophone, one play the clarinet. But I can't think of those guys, man. Been so long.
Well, that looks like a mate. End of the tape. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
